summary: BBN's host status report for January 31 to February 11, 1972. It lists hosts excluded from daily testing. It was replaced by RFC 315.

eli5.summary: A check on which network computers were up in early February.

questions: how did early arpanet monitor availability
subtitle: Checking which network hosts were working in February 1972

tldr.problem: Early ARPANET operators needed to know which computers on the network were functioning as servers so other sites could use them.
tldr.mechanism: BBN performed daily testing of network hosts from January 31 to February 11, 1972, recording whether each host was dead, half-open, open, refused, or timed out.
tldr.outcome: The report provided a snapshot of network availability, helping users find working services during the early days of packet-switched networking.

today: RFC 315 replaced this host status report, as BBN continued monitoring the growing ARPANET. These early status reports were the first systematic attempt to track network availability.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
RFC 306 reports on host status for the ARPANET from January 31 to February 11, 1972. The network at this time consisted of a small number of university and research computers connected through Interface Message Processors (IMPs). BBN, a key network contractor, conducted daily testing to determine whether each host was accessible.

The report excludes certain hosts from daily testing: hosts not expected to function as network servers within two weeks (such as prototype systems and machines under development), and hosts that were user-only machines or Terminal IMPs reserved for gathering network statistics.
sections.eli5: The ARPANET was just a few years old, and only a handful of computer centers were connected. BBN kept checking which ones were working each day so people would know where they could send their jobs.

sections.title: Host Categories
sections.content:
The status tables exclude machines falling into two categories. The first category includes hosts not expected to serve the network regularly for at least two weeks, such as research prototype systems. The second category includes hosts intended to be users only: Terminal IMPs present in the network (at AMES, MITRE, NBS, and BBN), the Network Control Center (address 5) used for statistics gathering, and machines at RAND, Harvard, Illinois, and NBS configured as user-only systems.

Hosts like UCLA, SRI, UCSB, UTAH, MIT, Stanford, SDC, and others were the operational servers on the network during this period.
sections.eli5: Some computers were set up just to receive data from the network (user-only), while others were ready to let other sites use them (servers). The report focused on the server machines.

sections.title: Status Codes
sections.content:
The daily testing used five status codes to report each host's condition:

  • O (Open): The host opened a connection and was accessible to users.
  • D (Dead): The host was either dead or inaccessible from the BBN Terminal IMP, possibly due to network partitioning or local IMP failure.
  • H (Half Open): The host opened a connection but then immediately closed it or did not respond further.
  • R (Refused): The host returned a CLS to the initial RFC (connection establishment request).
  • T (Time out): The host did not complete connection establishment (ICP) and open within 60 seconds.
sections.eli5: O meant the computer was ready. D meant it was broken or unreachable. H meant it started to listen but then went quiet. R meant it said no. T meant it was too slow to answer.
